match_question_text: Which of the following compounds will react with Tollen’s Reagent?

set.explanation_long: Tollen's reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) selectively oxidizes aldehydes, producing a silver mirror, but does not react with ketones (like 2-butanone or acetone) or carboxylic acids (like acetic acid). Among the four choices, only CH3CHO (acetaldehyde) is an aldehyde, so it is the only one that gives a positive Tollen's test. The printed UHS key marks B (2-butanone), but ketones do not reduce Tollens' reagent, so C is kept.

Which one of the following compounds show cis-trans isomerism?

set.explanation_short: 1-Bromo-2-chloropropene (BrCH=C(Cl)CH₃) has two different groups on each carbon of its double bond, so it shows cis-trans isomerism; the other three are terminal alkenes with a =CH₂ end.
set.explanation_long: Geometric (cis-trans) isomerism needs restricted rotation about a C=C bond and two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon. In 1-bromo-2-chloropropene, BrCH=C(Cl)–CH₃, carbon 1 carries H and Br and carbon 2 carries Cl and CH₃, so Br and Cl can lie on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans). Propene, 1-butene and 1-hexene all end in =CH₂, whose two identical hydrogens rule out cis-trans isomers. (The paper prints option C as '1-bromo-2-chloropropane', which has no double bond; C is the keyed option and is shown with the intended alkene name.)
set.explanation_trick: Look at both carbons of the C=C: if either one carries two identical groups (such as =CH₂), there are no cis-trans isomers.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 1-butene, CH₂=CH–CH₂CH₃, has two H atoms on carbon 1.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 1-hexene is also a terminal alkene with a =CH₂ end.
explanation_options.c: Correct — BrCH=C(Cl)CH₃ has different groups on both double-bond carbons, giving cis and trans forms.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃, has two H atoms on carbon 1.

match_question_text: In plants, the red light favours:

set.explanation_short: Plants grown under red light elongate (grow taller), whereas blue light suppresses cell elongation — so red light favours elongation of cells.
set.explanation_long: The quality (colour) of light changes the pattern of growth. Blue light, detected by cryptochromes, strongly inhibits the elongation of stem cells, so plants kept under blue light are short and compact. Under red light this inhibition is missing and cells elongate, so the plants grow tall. This is the textbook effect of light quality on growth and the answer in the UHS key.
set.explanation_trick: Blue light keeps plants short; red light lets their cells elongate.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — cell differentiation is not the effect of light colour described in textbooks.
explanation_options.b: Correct — red light favours elongation of cells; blue light inhibits it.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — maturation of cells is not the effect attributed to red light.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — enhancement of cell division is not the effect attributed to red light.

match_question_text: A large group of parasitic protozoa, some of which causes various diseases such as malaria to humans, are:
Which of the following components is less resistant to decay?

set.explanation_short: Starch is the least resistant to decay — it is a storage carbohydrate that almost every microbe can digest, whereas lignin, chitin and cellulose are tough structural polymers.
set.explanation_long: Decomposers break down materials at very different rates. Starch, a storage polysaccharide of α-glucose, is hydrolysed by amylases produced by a huge range of bacteria and fungi, so it decays quickly. Cellulose (β-glucose) and chitin (with nitrogen-containing sugars) are structural polymers that only specialised organisms can digest, and lignin is the most decay-resistant of all. (The printed UHS key marks C, chitin, but chitin is far more resistant to decay than starch.)
set.explanation_trick: Storage molecules (starch) are built to be broken down; structural molecules (lignin, chitin, cellulose) are built to last.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — lignin is the most decay-resistant natural polymer listed.
explanation_options.b: Correct — starch is readily digested by most decomposers, so it is the least resistant to decay.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — chitin is a tough structural polymer digested only by organisms with chitinase.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — cellulose resists decay and is digested only by organisms with cellulase.
